Subject: Scheduling challenge for a multi‑mode, resource‑shared project

Overview
We are planning a project with multiple interdependent activities that draw on shared, renewable resources and must be delivered within a fixed budget. Each activity can be delivered in one of several execution modes. These modes trade time against cost and resource usage: faster options generally cost more and may tie up more resources, while slower options cost less but extend duration. We must select exactly one mode per activity and set start dates so the overall plan finishes as early as possible without breaching timing, resource, or budget constraints.

Execution modes and non‑preemption
- Each activity has predefined execution modes with distinct durations, resource requirements, and costs.
- We will commit to one mode per activity; partial mode changes are not allowed.
- Activities, once started, must run to completion without interruption.

Dependencies and timing requirements
- Activities follow defined finish‑to‑start dependencies. Successors must wait at least the specified minimum delay after their predecessors finish.
- Some dependencies also carry maximum delays, requiring the successor to start within a specified window after the predecessor finishes.
- Certain activities have earliest allowed start times (release dates).
- Some activities have hard completion deadlines that cannot be missed.

Resource sharing and the conservative safety rule
- The project uses multiple renewable resource types, each with a fixed capacity. When an activity completes, its assigned resources return to the pool.
- To avoid overloads, we apply a conservative safety rule for activities that are not linked by precedence: if there exists even one combination of their execution modes and one resource for which their combined requirement would exceed that resource’s capacity, those two activities must not overlap in time. They must be explicitly sequenced, with one finishing before the other starts.
- This rule applies even if other mode combinations for the same pair would fit. The mere possibility of overload is sufficient to require sequencing.
- This is the only resource safeguard we will use. We will not perform an additional “at all times” capacity check beyond these pairwise sequencing decisions.

Budget and cost control
- The sum of the costs of the selected modes across all activities must stay within the fixed project budget.
- Selecting faster modes can shorten the plan but draws more budget; slower modes reduce spending but may create schedule pressure from deadlines and dependencies.

Planning implications
- Mode selection and start time choices must simultaneously satisfy precedence requirements, minimum/maximum inter‑task delays, release dates, and deadlines.
- The safety rule forces sequencing among certain independent activities regardless of the modes we ultimately pick, which can introduce critical path trade‑offs.
- The planning team will need to identify where paying for speed yields the greatest schedule benefit within the budget, while respecting timing windows and the required sequencing of potentially conflicting activities.

Goal
Build a feasible plan that selects one execution mode per activity and sequences all work to minimize total project duration while staying within budget and complying with all timing and resource rules.

Next steps
- Confirm scope, dependencies, and timing constraints with task owners.
- Validate resource capacities and the mode catalog (durations, resource needs, and costs).
- Identify all independent activity pairs that must be sequenced by the safety rule.
- Run schedule scenarios to evaluate time‑cost trade‑offs and propose a baseline plan and budget profile for approval.
